description_full: HP Inc. provides personal computing, printing, 3D printing, hybrid work, gaming, and other related technologies in the United States and internationally. The company operates through three segments: Personal Systems, Printing, and Corporate Investments. The Personal Systems segment offers commercial and consumer desktops and notebooks, workstations, thin clients, retail point-of-sale systems, displays, software, hybrid systems, and endpoint security and services, as well as lifecycle services, including support and deployment, configurations, and extended warranty services. The Printing segment provides consumer and commercial printer hardware, supplies, and solutions, as well as office and home printing solutions; and focuses on graphics, 3D printing, and personalization solutions for the commercial and industrial markets. The Corporate Investments segment is involved in the business incubation and investment projects. It serves small- and medium-sized businesses, public sector, and enterprises. The company was formerly known as Hewlett-Packard Company and changed its name to HP Inc. in October 2015. HP Inc. was founded in 1939 and is headquartered in Palo Alto, California.

financial_summary: HP Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $25.7B market cap on $55.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -4% over the past three years and -6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 67% against a 8% cost of capital — a 59-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 21% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2.8B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.4×.

Management returns a meaningful 7.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.25x its revenue share).
It accounts for 1.3% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-15.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 27% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 47% and a beta of 1.02, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $413.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 38% in the 2022 bear market and 48% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 53% below its DCF fair value of $60.87, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $47.08 to $81.60 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 10.9 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 7.1 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 9.2 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 73% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 10.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $27.52 on average, 3% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 67% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 59pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.50).
It runs a 21% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.46x.
It spends 2.9% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($3.7B of cash against $9.7B of debt), with interest covered 7.4x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.68 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.77 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
It runs on negative working capital (-42 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.2% over 3 years, -0.5% over 5 years and -6.1% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 37% of profits supports about 24.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.01, a backlog worth 8% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 11%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 1.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $3.4M sold).
It returns 7.6% a year to shareholders (3.3% in buybacks and 4.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 60 consecutive years, raising it 1.8% a year over the last five.
